SPIE SA (SPIE-FR): investment memo

SPIE: a well-run German-grid compounder de-rated for its French listing, whose consensus EPS must fall before the multiple recovers on a known date

Written 4 November 2026 for Richard. SPIE's earnings are compounding within a narrow range of outcomes, its share price is being set by French sovereign yields, and the reward lies in a multiple whose catalyst, the French presidential election of April to May 2027, has a date. Definitions, price dates and the model's basis are in the end notes.

The decision: build the position in tranches around three known dates, not before them

  1. Now to April 2027: consensus cuts FY2027 EPS by 5% to 7% for mechanical reasons, while every operating report confirms the case.
  2. 5 March 2027: the ROFA purchase price allocation shows whether SPIE overpaid for its largest 2026 acquisition.
  3. April to May 2027: the French presidential election decides whether the multiple can return from its trough band to its ten-year median.

#0 Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

1

SPIE is a good business whose share price has been set by its French listing, not by its numbers. Since June, SPIE's two-year-forward P/E has fallen about 20% while FY2027 consensus EPS has not moved. Deutsche Bank measures a correlation of -0.88 between SPIE's multiple and the French ten-year government bond yield in 2026 (R-squared 0.77), against +0.47 over the prior decade. France provides 32% of SPIE's revenue and about 28% of its EBITA, yet the market has applied a French country discount to the whole share.

2

SPIE's operating engine is accelerating, and the Q3 2026 sales report has just shown the market. Group organic growth reached 4.7% in Q3 (consensus 3.6%), after -0.9% in Q1 and 3.1% in Q2. Germany grew 5.2% organically on a record grid order book, France returned to +0.3% after -1.9%, and the 2026 acquisitions added 9.0% of revenue growth. Revenue, EBITA and cash are the well-founded part of the case: 85% of each year's revenue is visible at the start of the year, 70% to 75% of revenue is maintenance work, the EBITA margin has risen every year since 2020, and cash conversion has exceeded 100% in every year since 2015 except 2021.

3

Consensus is wrong at the EPS line, and the error is mechanical, dated and explainable. Three items below EBITA turned against EPS at once in 2026: 3.37m new shares from the early redemption of the ORNANE convertible bond (2% of the share count); two new bonds at 3.875% and 4.875% replacing convertible funding that cost 2%, which add about EUR 30m of annual interest by FY2027; and the French corporate tax surcharge, which the draft 2027 budget extends. The model's FY2027 EPS of EUR 3.15 is 9% below the EUR 3.46 consensus, even though the model's FY2027 EBITA is 1% above consensus. The brokers will close the gap by cutting their EPS estimates between now and the FY2026 results on 5 March 2027. Expect net EPS revisions to be negative for two quarters while every operating report confirms the case.

4

The German grid is the most important single driver of the case, and its risk lies in the timing of the spending, not in whether it happens. TenneT's German capex rises from about EUR 5bn in 2025 to about EUR 14bn in 2027; Amprion plans EUR 42bn and E.ON EUR 48bn of investment to 2030; Germany's EUR 500bn federal infrastructure fund disburses from 2027; and regulated allowed returns rise from 4.13% towards about 6.5%. SPIE is the purest listed exposure to this spending and earns margins of 15% to 16% on German high-voltage work. Because transformer lead times are 128 to 160 weeks, grid orders reach revenue over one to two years, so 2027 and 2028 will carry more of the acceleration than 2026.

5

No broker has reconciled the price SPIE paid for ROFA with the multiple SPIE says it paid. SPIE paid EUR 682.8m for ROFA, a factory and logistics automation business with about EUR 430m of revenue at a "high single-digit" margin, which implies EBITA of roughly EUR 34m to 40m. The company described the price as a "high single-digit multiple", and Morgan Stanley built its forecast of "mid-single-digit EPS accretion" on an assumed price of EUR 250m to 330m. Neither statement fits a EUR 682.8m price unless ROFA came with several hundred million euros of net cash or customer advances. The purchase price allocation published with the FY2026 results on 5 March 2027 will settle the question. ROFA is only 4% of group EBITA, so the EBITA path survives either answer; SPIE's reputation as a disciplined acquirer may not.

6

SPIE's 2028 margin target and its organic growth target are one question. At an incremental margin of 11% to 12%, 3% organic growth adds about 11 bps of EBITA margin a year, which supplies most of the 36 bps needed to reach the 8.0% margin target for 2028. At SPIE's ten-year average organic growth of 1.8%, the margin target is missed by about 15 bps. I expect organic growth to average about 2.6% over 2025 to 2028 against the 3% to 4% target, the organic target to be reframed at the 2027 Capital Markets Day, and the margin target to be met through a richer business mix.

7

The coming nine months are a sequence of confirmations with one binary event in the middle. The Q3 sales are done. Next come the Share For You employee share settlement (3 December 2026); the FY2026 results, with the ROFA purchase price allocation, the run-rate of net financial costs and the treatment of the tax surcharge (5 March 2027); the French presidential election (April to May 2027); the H1 2027 results, with the first full half-year of ROFA (July 2027); and a 2027 Capital Markets Day with 2030 targets. The market will learn about the EPS cuts first, then the ROFA answer, then the election result, then the new roadmap, so the narrative gets worse before it gets better.

8

The returns at the guideline fair multiple are returns at a trough multiple. The model's returns of +2.7% to December 2027 and +17.9% to June 2029 are computed at a two-year-forward P/E of 10.49x, which lies inside the stock's ten-year band between the "crash" level (9.9x) and the "conservative" level (11.2x); the Phases page now gives a guideline of 10.94x. At the ten-year median multiple of 11.8x, the same earnings give about +15% and +31%. The reward in this case therefore sits in the multiple, and the catalyst for the multiple has a date and lies outside management's control.

9

The setup fits the pattern "cause for concern clearing in a low-cyclicality business on a low-quartile multiple", recognisably but not crisply. The concern is exogenous (French sovereign risk), it clears on a date six months away, and a second, smaller concern, the rebasing of consensus EPS, must pass first. Buying before March 2027 means owning the shares through the EPS cut; buying between March and the election means taking the election binary at a known trough multiple, with ROFA's price already verified. Choosing between those two entry windows is the practical decision.

10

My ratings: strength of the thesis's change forces B; robustness of the foundations B; fit and crispness of the setup C; riskiness of the case C. The Rater's scores for the same four measures, given in #13, are 64, 72, 58 and 63, all in the C band.

#1 Tailwinds in the operating environment, and the headwinds

Conclusion: strong and lengthening structural tailwinds act on SPIE's earnings, the legacy drags are small and fading, and the one large headwind, French country risk, acts on the multiple rather than on volumes.

Evidence: the grid. European grid investment, above all in Germany, is the structural driver. European grid spending is expected to reach about EUR 500bn over 2025 to 2030, against EUR 320bn historically, and the German transmission operators will spend at least EUR 14bn a year by 2032. Since April 2026, Germany has ordered its grid-connection queue by project readiness, which moves viable projects to the front. Germany's fifth regulatory period (RP5) lifts allowed returns on grid assets from 4.13% to about 6.5%, and E.ON is lobbying for 8%. Transmission and distribution work was 34% of SPIE's group revenue in 2024. German high-voltage and city-network work is over 30% of SPIE's German revenue, or about 11% to 12% of the group.

Evidence: the secondary drivers. Data centres are about 3% of SPIE's revenue; German data-centre capacity is forecast to grow 70% by 2030, and SPIE serves mid-sized co-location operators, delivering about 75% of each project's value in-house. French nuclear work comes from EDF's Grand Carénage reactor life-extension programme, with a decision on the new EPR2 reactors expected in late 2026. Battery storage work is supported by a European framework agreement with Tesla. Customers who cannot hire engineers are outsourcing whole technical departments to SPIE on five-to-ten-year frameworks.

Evidence: Q3 2026. The Q3 sales confirmed the direction. Germany grew 5.2% organically with a record order book; North-Western Europe grew 12.5% as Dutch high-voltage projects entered intensive execution; Central Europe grew 5.8%. After a weather-hit Q1, group organic growth for the first nine months of 2026 was 2.3%.

Evidence: the headwinds. SPIE's headwinds come from legacy businesses and country-level cycles, and they are small. French fibre roll-out work is running off, from about EUR 150m of revenue in 2025 to EUR 120m in 2026; the run-off subtracts about 1 percentage point from French growth and fades mechanically through 2027. In French tertiary (commercial) building, competitors lead on price, and SPIE gives up volume to hold its margin. Global Services Energy, 4% of revenue, is losing Middle East maintenance work because of the Iran conflict and is pruning sub-Saharan contracts; its organic growth was -6.8% in Q3 and is expected to be worse in Q4. The Eurozone construction PMI stands at 43.4.

Two constraints bind in every market. Skilled labour is scarce: Germany has 615 vacancies for every 100 unemployed electrical engineers. Equipment is slow: lead times of 128 to 160 weeks for switchgear and transformers set the pace at which orders become revenue.

Competition for customers is rational and easing. Equans, the under-bidder of 2021 to 2023, is repairing its margin from 2.9% towards a 5.2% target, and VINCI Energies and Eiffage bid selectively. Competition for acquisition targets in Germany is intensifying: Brookfield, Eiffage and VINCI Energies (23 deals in nine months) are pushing bolt-on multiples from 6x to 7x EBITA towards 7x to 9x.

Inference. SPIE's demand is splitting in two. The structural part is strengthening and carries more than two years of contracted visibility; the cyclical and run-off part is weak but small and fading, and the structural part now dominates the outlook. Because labour and equipment, not demand, set the pace, the acceleration in reported organic growth will be gradual and long: 3% to 4% a year rather than the 7% to 8% that the German order book alone would suggest, lasting into the early 2030s. A gradual, long acceleration is the better shape for a compounder.

So what. The external environment supports SPIE's organic growth recovering from about 2.6% in FY2026 to 3% to 3.5% in FY2027 and FY2028, led by Germany, with France flat to slightly positive. The external environment does not, on its own, support a re-rating within six months, because the macro and country regime is acting on the multiple: the French ten-year spread over German Bunds was 137 to 171 bps in October, and a risk-off market is paying for equipment makers rather than installers.

Where I differ from the market. The sell-side agrees with me on the German story and is positive on it. I differ on its timing. Morgan Stanley now forecasts 4% organic growth for 2027 to 2029; I think 3% to 3.5% is the right central case, for two reasons. Q3's surge in North-Western Europe was project phasing that management itself said rolls off in Q4, and the German federal fund disbursed about 20% less than planned in 2026. The risk to my view is a faster conversion of orders into revenue, which would be an upgrade.

Counter-case. Three events would weaken the tailwind: a cut in German allowed returns that grid operators pass down to contractors; a financing freeze among hyperscale or co-location data-centre operators (credit spreads of the new "neocloud" operators are widening); and a French sovereign shock that freezes private capex, which Bernstein sizes at up to 25% of group sales (the non-recurring part). What would change my view: German organic growth below 4% for two consecutive quarters, or a visible rise in the subcontracted share of German grid work.

Score: 70, set by the Rater. A funded, regulated and multi-year external force reaches SPIE's core business: TenneT's German transmission capex roughly triples by 2027, allowed returns rise from 4.13% towards about 6.5%, and grid work is about a third of group revenue, with data centres, French nuclear and engineering outsourcing as further legs. Labour shortages and equipment lead times of 128 to 160 weeks cap the force, so organic growth rises only from about 2.6% to 3% to 3.5%, and French fibre run-off, price-led French tertiary work and Global Services Energy take a fading slice. Consensus sales growth, at the 50th percentile, does not yet show the force, because the lag from order to revenue is mechanical. I go above the group's 64 because the force is written into regulation and contracts rather than forecast, but it reaches only part of sales, so it sits just below Eckert & Ziegler (72) and well above Odfjell Drilling (62).

#2 Internally-driven change forces, and the problems

Conclusion: an orderly succession, a raised margin ambition and a balance sheet put to work in Germany are strongly positive at the EBITA line, but SPIE's own 2026 financing choices dilute EPS, and one large acquisition price remains unverified.

Evidence: leadership and targets. Markus Holzke became CEO on 1 May 2026, succeeding Gauthier Louette after 23 years. Holzke built SPIE Germany from about EUR 650m of revenue in 2014 to EUR 3.6bn in 2025, and he reviewed over 90 active projects in his first three months as CEO. The Chairman and CEO roles were split, with Patrick Jeantet as non-executive Chairman. The CFO, Jérôme Vanhove (in post since 2022, with 15 years in strategy and M&A), stays. In March 2026 SPIE raised its 2028 margin target from "at least 7.7%" to 8.0%, with EBITA above EUR 1bn.

Evidence: acquisitions. 2026 is SPIE's largest acquisition year since 2017: about EUR 800m of acquired annual revenue for about EUR 1.03bn of spending. ROFA (factory and logistics automation, about EUR 430m of revenue) is over half of the acquired revenue; SGS Industrial Services (about EUR 180m, a margin above 10%, 800 technicians) is the second-largest deal. SPIE funded the spending with a EUR 600m bond at 3.875% and allowed leverage to touch 2.1x net debt to EBITDA at June. Fitch upgraded SPIE to investment grade (BBB-) in April.

Evidence: financing and ownership. SPIE redeemed its ORNANE convertible bond early on 20 October and replaced it with a EUR 500m bond at 4.875% and 3,365,843 new shares. The Share For You 2026 employee offer drew over 27,000 employees in 18 countries at EUR 35.36 a share, taking employee ownership to about 9.2%. The anchor shareholders, Peugeot Invest and Bpifrance, have left; BlackRock, at about 8%, is the only external holder above 5%. There is no activist and no disclosed short position.

Evidence: the problems. SPIE's problems sit below EBITA and in project execution.

  • Dilution and interest: the ORNANE swap adds about 2% to the share count and about EUR 13m to 15m of annual interest from FY2027; Deutsche Bank estimates that the swap cuts FY2027 EPS by 4%.
  • Share-based pay: IFRS 2 share-based charges of EUR 59.8m, about 7% of EBITA, are excluded from SPIE's adjusted figures, whereas Bilfinger includes its own.
  • Alignment: executives and managers own 0.4% of the capital, against a peer average of about 2%, and there is no clawback.
  • Execution: the new project-heavy segments have had setbacks, namely a Cologne data centre staffed by two SPIE employees and subcontractors, and Dutch substations six months late with cost overruns of 20% to 25%. The direct-labour ratio in those segments is 65% to 70%, against 75% to 80% at VINCI Energies.
  • Legal: a first-instance bribery conviction (EUR 1.5m of fines, for conduct over ten years old) is under appeal.
  • Weather: Central Europe's H1 margin fell 90 bps to 2.4%.

Inference. The internal changes amount to a large change of person, a small change of policy, and a step-up in using the balance sheet for growth rather than for shareholder returns. These changes are improvements in continuity: well resourced and credible at the EBITA line, but partly offset at the EPS line by financing, dilution and tax costs that management chose. The ORNANE refinancing, in particular, was opportunistic rather than forced.

So what. Forecast EBITA growth of about 10% in FY2026 and FY2027 with confidence. Build EPS from EBITA line by line, and expect EPS growth to lag EBITA growth by 2 to 3 percentage points a year until FY2028. Treat Holzke's first roadmap, at the 2027 Capital Markets Day, as the most likely occasion for a higher mid-term margin and cash ambition, set in the company's habit of floors that are then beaten.

Where I differ from the market. The market reads ROFA and SGS together as an "accretive German industrial cluster". I read ROFA as a price that needs verifying and as a cyclical exposure that the grid narrative omits: 30% of ROFA's business is automotive (Volkswagen, Porsche, BMW, Audi). SGS is the better deal of the two. None of the nine brokers covering SPIE has reconciled ROFA's price with the multiple the company stated.

Counter-case. Holzke's integration record at group level is six months old, and SPIE is absorbing its largest acquisition cohort since SAG, which diluted margins for five years from 2015, during a leadership succession. What would change my view: a ROFA purchase price allocation showing EUR 300m or more of acquired cash or advances, which would reconcile the price and support the accretion claim; or a German segment margin in H1 2027 below the 5.8% of H1 2026, which would signal integration friction.

Score: 62, set by the Rater. The company's own actions are clearly positive at EBITA: an orderly succession to the CEO who built SPIE Germany from EUR 650m to EUR 3.6bn, the 2028 margin target raised to 8.0% with EBITA above EUR 1bn, the largest acquisition year since 2017 (about EUR 800m of acquired revenue, about 8% of the group) and an investment-grade rating. The company's own choices give part of the gain back: the ORNANE refinancing adds 2% to the share count and about EUR 30m of interest, so EPS lags EBITA by 2 to 3 points a year, and the new project-heavy segments have had overruns. That is more ambition than Richard's "gently positive but mediocre" CVS (55) and close to OEM International's (66) turn into an active acquirer, but the dilution keeps it below OEM International. I sit slightly above the group's 57 because the size of the acquisition step-up is itself a large change force.

#3 Value chain, industry structure, business model, financial profile, management

Conclusion: SPIE has a favourable and only moderately fragile industry structure, a durable stack of moderate competitive advantages, a top-of-peer financial profile and a credible, risk-averse management; the trade-off is that the same risk aversion caps organic growth at about 3%.

Industry structure: two different markets. Germany (35% of SPIE's revenue, a market of EUR 100bn to 120bn) is extremely fragmented. The top four firms hold about 9%, small local firms hold 91.5%, and SPIE, at about 3%, is number one by a hair over VINCI Energies. That fragmentation is SPIE's acquisition runway and its guard against national price wars. France (32% of revenue) is a concentrated oligopoly in which the top five hold about 45% and SPIE is number four at about 5%, behind VINCI Energies, Equans and Eiffage. Pricing is rational among the French leaders; the swing factor is residential contractors spilling into tertiary work.

Customers, entry barriers and competitors. SPIE's customers are large, regulated or mission-critical: energy and utilities are 25% of revenue and public bodies 14%, SPIE has close to 30,000 customers, the top ten account for 18%, and retention on maintenance contracts is above 90%. Prequalification requirements (for live substations and nuclear sites) and a three-to-five-year training pipeline for grid crews keep new entrants out; the entrants that matter are financial consolidators bidding for the same acquisition targets. SPIE's competitors put margin first: VINCI Energies earns 7.4% to 7.8%, Eiffage Énergie Systèmes 6.2%, Equans about 4.4% (targeting 5.2%), and Bilfinger 5.5%, in recovery after a profit warning. Labour scarcity sets a floor under prices; as an October expert call put it, "pricing increasingly follows execution capacity".

Business model and moat. SPIE has no fortress, but it has a stack of six moderate, reinforcing advantages, most of them widening.

  1. Funding: working capital is -34 days of revenue (EUR -975.5m at end-2025), against positive days at Bilfinger and Bravida, and capex is below 1% of revenue, so growth and acquisitions fund themselves.
  2. Prequalified scarce skills in high-voltage and nuclear work, evidenced by 15% to 16% margins on German grid work and EDF contracts of up to 17 years.
  3. Local density across close to 1,000 branches.
  4. A recruiting and retention edge: voluntary staff turnover of 5.9%, about 1,200 hires a year through employee referrals, a record number of apprentices, and employee ownership.
  5. Sticky multi-year frameworks.
  6. An acquisition engine of more than 90 deals, which frees working capital worth about 1x EBITA from each target within a year.

The acquisition arbitrage is the one advantage narrowing at the margin, because entry multiples are rising and ROFA's price suggests that SPIE itself is paying up for scale. SPIE captures its scale economies rather than sharing them with customers (there is no Costco-type loop), so the moat depends on skills remaining scarce; the length of the training pipeline and the strength of grid demand make continued scarcity likely for years.

Financial profile. SPIE has the best margin among the large European peers: 7.6%, rising by 40 bps a year from 2023 to 2025. Cash conversion has exceeded 100% every year since 2015 except 2021 (108% in 2025), and free cash flow runs at 1.1x to 1.4x adjusted net income. Post-tax ROCE including goodwill is about 13% to 14%, and returns on tangible capital are far above 50%. Leverage was 1.3x net debt to EBITDA at end-2025 and 2.1x at the June seasonal peak, and is heading to about 1.7x at end-2026 and about 1x by 2029, even with EUR 350m a year of bolt-on acquisitions. The profile has two blemishes: excluding share-based pay flatters adjusted EPS by about 9%, and goodwill makes up EUR 4.4bn of EUR 7.4bn of non-current assets.

Management. SPIE's management is a disciplined team of operators and capital allocators with a congruent culture: margin over volume, decentralised branches with central signing thresholds, and a long-term incentive plan weighted 55% to EBITA growth and cash conversion and 25% to relative total shareholder return, which pays nothing below the peer median. Management's goals are credible rather than stretching. Its "ultra-conservative" bidding framework deliberately sits 150 to 200 bps of organic growth below volume-oriented peers; organic growth averaged 1.8% over 2015 to 2025 and was below the peer median in 18 of 33 quarters. Capital allocation is enlightened in its chosen channel (bolt-on acquisitions at a cited 17% ROCE for the 2019 to 2022 cohort) and passive on buybacks, which only offset dilution even though the stock trades on an 8% to 9% free cash flow yield.

Where I differ from the market. Consensus and the brokers treat SPIE as a high-quality compounder, and I agree on its cash, margin and moat. I weight the subcontractor link more heavily than they do. Subcontracting and temporary labour exceed 56% of SPIE's total expenses; subcontracting is the sector's classic channel for leaking the margin from scarce skills to the sub-tier, and SPIE's two documented project setbacks occurred exactly there. Deutsche Bank calculates a 9.1% post-tax return on SPIE's cumulative acquisition spending over 2016 to 2025, against management's 17% on a selected cohort; I believe Deutsche Bank's more sceptical figure.

Counter-case and what would change my view. If the labour market loosened in a European recession, the price floor and the scarcity moat would weaken together. The first sign would be revenue per employee growing more slowly than staff cost per employee at the FY2026 results.

Score: 63, set by the Rater. The qualitative parts are good but not exceptional. Germany is a fragmented market that SPIE consolidates, and France is a rational oligopoly in which SPIE is only number four. Moderate, mostly widening advantages come from prequalified grid and nuclear crews, a recruiting edge, frameworks with retention above 90%, and -34 days of working capital that funds growth. Management is disciplined but risk-averse, with organic growth averaging 1.8%. The Universe figures understate the financial profile: gross margin (6th percentile), EBITDA margin (19th percentile) and ROIC of 4.1% (30th percentile) reflect a labour-services model and EUR 4.4bn of goodwill. Cash conversion (93rd percentile), returns on tangible capital above 50% and margins at the top of the peer group are the truer reading, though Deutsche Bank's 9.1% return on cumulative acquisition spending is only about the cost of capital, and 56% of costs go to subcontracting. I place it in line with the groups (55 to 63), a little above the comparable MITIE (54) and just below Linea Directa (64).

#4 Conservatism of guidance, management of expectations, and the record

Conclusion: SPIE's guidance is conservative and reliable on the lines it covers, with a clean record of setting floors for margin and cash and beating them; the exposure is EPS, which the company does not guide and which consensus has 7% to 9% too high for FY2026 and FY2027.

Evidence: the guidance. FY2026 guidance is qualitative ("strong total revenue growth and continued EBITA margin expansion", with cash conversion of about 100%) and was reiterated on 30 October. When asked, the CEO declined to reconfirm a 20 bps step-up in the second-half margin, saying instead that the company never wants to give up margin gains. The 2028 framework is specific: an 8.0% margin, EBITA above EUR 1bn, total growth of 7% to 9% a year including 3% to 4% organic, cumulative free cash flow above EUR 2bn over 2025 to 2028, leverage below 2.0x and a 40% payout.

Evidence: the record. SPIE's pattern is to set a floor, firm it at mid-year, and meet or beat it by 0 to 10 bps. The record table below sets out each case. Organic growth is the exception: repeated 3% to 4% ambitions have produced a 1.8% average.

Evidence: consensus and the sell-side. Consensus EBITA margins for FY2026 to FY2028 are 7.8%, 7.9% and 7.9%, slightly under the 8.0% target, and consensus FY2028 EBITA of EUR 988m is under the EUR 1bn target, because the brokers model no acquisitions after 2026. Of the eleven brokers, ten (85%) rate SPIE a Buy; the median target price is EUR 57, and RBC is the lone Hold, at EUR 45. FY2027 consensus EPS has moved 0% over one month, -1% over three months and +4% over twelve months, and EBITDA consensus has risen 9% over twelve months.

Inference. SPIE's guidance is conservative on margin and cash, fair to demanding on organic growth, and silent on EPS. On the model's path, the cumulative free cash flow target will be beaten by about EUR 400m; the margin target is reachable through business mix even if organic growth disappoints; and the organic growth average is the target most likely to be missed and reframed. Management keeps sell-side expectations where it wants them on the lines it guides. It has no mechanism to manage the lines it does not guide, and EPS is the line on which consensus has drifted too high.

“They always beat on what they guide.”The exposure is the line nobody guides: EPS.

So what. Treat SPIE's targets as floors for margin and cash, and as a range closer to a ceiling for organic growth. Expect guidance to be met at every event over the next 18 months (about 85% probability) and firmed at one or two of them (the H1 2027 results and the Capital Markets Day). Expect the same events to bring consensus EPS cuts of 2% to 3% for FY2026 and 5% to 7% for FY2027, as seven or eight of the eleven brokers enter the October share count and the new bond coupons. Jefferies has already cut its FY2027 EPS by 2% and Deutsche Bank by 4%; Bernstein has entered the new shares and the bond and left its estimates unchanged.

Where I differ from the market. The sell-side is crowded long and reads SPIE's record as "they always beat". I read the record as "they always beat on what they guide". Consensus EPS growth of 15.6% for FY2026 and 11.2% for FY2027 requires the conversion of EBITA into adjusted net income to rise from 57.7% to 62%; that rise has no precedent in SPIE's own accounts and runs against every below-EBITA item that moved in 2026. On the operating lines, I side with Bernstein's 7.9% FY2026 margin rather than the 7.8% median, given the 11.9% drop-through of incremental revenue to EBITA in H1.

Counter-case. Holzke reiterated guidance in July despite a beat and refused to quantify the second-half margin in October; that behaviour could signal a CEO who guides less, rather than one who sandbags. If so, the mid-year "firming" steps that have historically been upgrade catalysts will become rarer. What would change my view: a quantified FY2027 margin floor in March 2027, which would show the habit continues; or any company guidance on interest, tax or share count, which would mean the company, rather than the brokers, closes the EPS gap.

Score: 68, set by the Rater. On the lines it guides, the record is a clean pattern of setting a floor and beating it: the 2025 margin target was reached in 2023, the margin came in at 7.2% against "at least 7.1%" and 7.6% against "at least 7.6%", cash conversion was 122% and 108% against a 100% guide, and the 2028 target was raised a year after it was set. Organic growth has repeatedly missed its 3% to 4% ambition (a 1.8% average, with misses in Q3 2025 and Q1 2026). The company does nothing to keep EPS consensus conservative, and consensus sits 7% to 9% too high for FY2026 and FY2027, which is why the sell-side group scores 44 against the guidance group's 62. That puts it below Kerry's (74) similar record of delivering within bands, and level with or just under Linea Directa (69).

#5 Pricing power, operating leverage, financial leverage, cost scope and feedback loops

Conclusion: revenue growth converts into EBITA growth at about 1.5x, through contribution-margin leverage and pass-through pricing, but in FY2026 and FY2027 EBITA growth converts into EPS growth at only about 0.85x; the lever nobody uses is the balance sheet itself.

Pricing. SPIE has demonstrated, not merely claimed, the power to pass costs through. Its EBITA margin rose from about 5% in 2020 to 7.6% in 2025 through 4% to 6% wage inflation; revenue per employee has grown faster than staff cost per employee for five years; about two-thirds of 2023's 8.4% organic growth was price; Dutch clients accepted rises of 5% to 10%; and customer retention stayed above 90%. Real pricing power, meaning price rises above cost inflation, is confined to grid, nuclear and complex co-location work and is worth perhaps 5 to 10 bps of group margin a year. Price contributes about 1.5 to 2 percentage points of revenue growth a year, so as wage inflation normalises, the 3% organic target now needs 1% to 1.5% of real volume growth, which only Germany has delivered. In French tertiary building SPIE cannot raise prices and gives up volume instead.

Operating leverage. SPIE's operating leverage comes from contribution margin, not from fixed costs. Purchases are 14% of operating costs, external services 43% (about EUR 1.8bn of it subcontracting) and employment 37%; truly fixed overhead is roughly 4% to 5% of revenue. The incremental margin on organic revenue runs at 11% to 12% (10.7% in FY2024, 11.7% to 11.9% in H1 2026, and a 2020 to 2025 average of 12.1% according to Deutsche Bank), against an average margin of 7.8%. As a result, 1% of revenue growth moves EBITA by about 1.5%, and 3% organic growth adds about 11 bps of margin a year.

The leverage is asymmetric, depending on how fast revenue falls. In 2020, revenue fell suddenly by 4.8% and the decremental margin was 27%, because SPIE kept its skilled crews; in a gradual slowdown SPIE releases subcontractors first, and the decremental margin is nearer 15% to 20%. A 2 percentage point shortfall in organic growth therefore costs about EUR 25m of EBITA if gradual and EUR 45m to 60m if sudden.

Financial leverage. SPIE's financial leverage is modest and largely fixed-rate: 86% of gross debt is at fixed rates, so a 50 bps move in interest rates changes costs by about EUR 3m. EBITA is about 1.17x pre-tax profit, so a 1% change in EBITA moves EPS by about 1.2%, and each EUR 10m of financial cost is worth about EUR 0.04 of EPS (1.2%). In FY2026 and FY2027 the direction is adverse: net financial items rise from about EUR 111m to about EUR 140m, before falling as debt is repaid. A EUR 600m term loan refinances in October 2027 at about 4% to 4.5%.

Cost scope. SPIE has little scope to cut costs, by design: there is no cost programme, overhead is lean, and integration synergies are described as "primarily commercial". Structural efficiency worth 15 to 25 bps of margin over three to four years is already inside the 8.0% target. The real value of the cost base is its flexibility in a downturn.

Feedback loops. Five loops shape SPIE's economics.

  • The self-funding acquisition loop is reinforcing, but its gain is falling. Negative working capital funds bolt-ons, the acquired working capital is optimised, and the acquired EBITA funds the next deal. EUR 350m of acquisitions bought EUR 45m to 70m of EBITA at past multiples of 5x to 8x, buys about EUR 38m at today's 9x, and would have bought only about EUR 18m to 20m at ROFA's implied multiple.
  • The labour loop reinforces price and caps volume.
  • The grid reference loop is reinforcing but gated by equipment: each award, such as TenneT's eight-year, five-substation framework, helps win the next.
  • The negative working-capital loop releases about EUR 9m of cash for every EUR 100m of organic growth and reverses only if revenue falls; a 5% revenue decline would absorb about EUR 50m.
  • The reflexive valuation loop is switched off. At 11.7x earnings, a buyback earns more than any acquisition priced above 12x, yet SPIE's buybacks only offset dilution. As leverage falls towards 1x by 2029, about EUR 1bn of headroom to 2.0x appears, about 14% of today's market value, and no model uses it.
The unused lever: about EUR 1bn of headroom to 2.0x leverage appears by 2029, about 14% of today's market value, and no model uses it.

Where I differ from the market. The brokers assume a drop-through of 9% to 10.5% on incremental revenue; SPIE's record says 11% to 12%, which implies modest upside to operating consensus. The market also treats EPS as if it grew in line with EBITA; in FY2026 and FY2027, EPS grows at only about 0.85x the rate of EBITA.

Counter-case and what would change my view. If subcontractor costs in grid and data-centre projects rise faster than contract indexation allows, 20 to 40 bps of margin could leak away; the MYR Group precedent lost 290 bps. A step back in the North-Western Europe or German margin in H1 2027 would be the evidence.

Score: 42, set by the Rater. Structurally this is contribution-margin leverage, not fixed-cost leverage. Only about 4% to 5% of revenue is truly fixed overhead and the incremental margin is 11% to 12% against a 7.8% average, so 1% more revenue gives about 1.5% more EBITA. Pass-through pricing is proven (the margin rose from about 5% to 7.6% through 4% to 6% wage inflation), but real price is worth only 5 to 10 bps a year. There is little cost scope, by design. Financial leverage is modest and moving against EPS (EBITA converts to EPS at about 0.85x in FY2026 and FY2027), and the acquisition loop still reinforces but buys less each year. The forecast ratio of EPS growth to revenue growth is only about 1.2x, against a Universe median near 2x. The topic sits a little above the low-gearing services peers Bravida (36) and MITIE (38) on the strength of proven pass-through and the self-funding loop, and below the group's 55, which leans on cash conversion rather than gearing.

#6 Forecast financials, and scope for higher growth and margins than the past

Conclusion: EBITA passes EUR 1bn in FY2028 within a narrow range of outcomes that leans slightly upward; EPS compounds at about 8% to 9% a year on the model's path, below consensus for two years for mechanical reasons and above it afterwards, with balance-sheet optionality from 2028 that no model includes.

The model's forecasts of record (update 2), EUR m except per-share figures:

The model's EPS is on the economic basis, with the French tax surcharge treated as a cost. If SPIE adds the surcharge back in its headline adjusted EPS, as the tax note in its interim report suggests, the company-basis figures are about EUR 0.10 higher in FY2026 and FY2027 (about EUR 2.99 and EUR 3.25). The end notes explain a basis break in the model's FY2025 EPS history.

The drivers behind the forecast lines. The table sets out the model's assumptions.

Two inputs I change for the Q3 sales. The model's inputs pre-date the 30 October Q3 report. Q3 revenue of EUR 2,886.8m grew 13.7% (organic 4.7%, scope 9.0%), against the model's second-half assumption of +10.4%. With Q4 organic growth near 3.3% (Morgan Stanley: 3.6%) and scope growth near 9% (a full quarter of ROFA and SGS, plus Clauser), H2 2026 revenue comes to about EUR 6.1bn (+13%) and FY2026 revenue to about EUR 11.27bn (+8.4%, in line with the EUR 11.24bn consensus), with FY2026 organic growth of about 2.6%. Carrying the higher base forward, with unchanged FY2027 organic growth of 3.0% and the same cadence of bolt-ons, gives FY2027 revenue of about EUR 12.19bn (+8.2%). I leave margins unchanged, because three factors offset the higher drop-through: the CEO's refusal to quantify the second-half margin step, the Q4 roll-off of North-Western Europe's project phasing, and the pruning of Global Services Energy. I scale depreciation and amortisation with revenue. The two changes add about 1% to EBITA and EPS in every year (FY2026 EPS about EUR 2.93, FY2027 about EUR 3.19, FY2028 about EUR 3.55) and change no conclusion.

Against the past. The next four years look like a slower, steadier and more cash-rich version of 2019 to 2025. In 2019 to 2025, adjusted EPS growth of about 11% a year was helped by deleveraging from 3.3x, a convertible bond costing 2%, and cash tax below the tax charge in the accounts; none of those helps repeat. The margin rose 160 bps from 6.0% to 7.6%, and 260 bps from the 2020 trough.

The scope for more. Double-digit EPS growth is available from FY2028 on the model's own path, and could arrive sooner if SPIE uses its balance-sheet headroom. Each EUR 300m of buybacks at about 11x to 12x earnings adds about 1.5% to EPS, and Deutsche Bank's scenario of EUR 1.0bn to 1.35bn a year of acquisitions gives 14% EPS accretion in FY2028. Margins above the past are achievable but bounded: precedent supports 8.0% to 8.5% by 2028 to 2029 (Bernstein's normalised margin is 8.4%), but no large multi-technical group in the sector has sustained a margin above 9%.

Where I differ from the market. On EBITA and cash, the model sits slightly above consensus, and well above it from FY2028, because consensus models no acquisitions after 2026 and no deleveraging either, which is internally inconsistent. On EPS, the model sits 7% to 9% below consensus to FY2027 for the three below-EBITA reasons. Consensus FY2027 EPS of EUR 3.46 lies above the top of the model's range of outcomes: bear case EUR 2.80, base case EUR 3.15 and bull case EUR 3.40 on the economic basis, with a base case of about EUR 3.23 on the company basis.

Counter-case and what would change my view. The model's EPS could be too low if ROFA came with large net cash (lower debt, lower interest), if the surcharge lapses after the election (FY2028 EPS +2.7%), or if management buys back stock at scale. What would change my view is the 5 March 2027 disclosure of four items: net financial items (model: about EUR 127m for FY2026), the surcharge and its treatment, the year-end diluted share count (model: about 174.6m), and ROFA's acquired cash.

Score: 68, set by the Rater. The 5% to 10% band gives C, and the measure is honest once the basis break in the model's EPS history is removed. I place it in the upper part of the band, not at the top: growth is close to the 10% line, and the margin path passes the company's best (7.6% to about 8.2%) and EUR 1bn of EBITA. But margin gains run at a quarter of the past pace, about half the revenue growth is bought, and EPS trails EBITA until FY2028 because of interest, dilution and the surcharge.

#7 Scope for upgrades to guidance, consensus and the narrative over 6 to 12 months

Conclusion: there is strong scope for upgrades to operating consensus, guidance and the longer-dated narrative, but a two-quarter mechanical cut to EPS consensus comes first, and the company can explain that cut in one slide; the risk/reward improves materially once the cut is through.

Guidance. SPIE will meet its guidance at every event (about 85% probability) and firm it at one or two. The most likely upgrades are a quantified FY2027 margin floor at the H1 2027 results in July, following the July 2025 precedent, and a 2030 roadmap at the 2027 Capital Markets Day with a margin of "at least 8.5%" and a higher cash target (about 65% probability). A statement on capital returns is possible (about 30%) and would be genuinely new.

Operating consensus. FY2026 organic growth consensus is already moving up after Q3 (Morgan Stanley: "expect cons to move up"). FY2026 EBITA margin consensus will settle at 7.8% to 7.9%. FY2028 EBITA consensus (EUR 988m) will rise towards and through EUR 1bn as the 2027 bolt-ons are announced; Clauser, in October, was the first of the next cohort.

EPS consensus. FY2027 EPS consensus will be cut first, from EUR 3.46 towards EUR 3.25 to 3.30 by April 2027, as the brokers' models enter the October share count, the two new coupons and, for some brokers, the surcharge. Consensus will then hold at the H1 2027 results, and FY2028 to FY2030 EPS will be raised with the roadmap and the deals. Net breadth of EPS revisions will turn negative for about two quarters, perhaps -60% to -80%, the first negative stretch since the confusion over the ORNANE in 2025. The share of Buy ratings may slip from 85% towards 70% to 75%, and target prices from EUR 57 towards EUR 50 to 54.

The narrative. The sell-side's narrative covers the German grid story and the French discount thoroughly, the below-EBITA costs only partially (two of nine brokers model them fully) and the ROFA price not at all. Two optical events help from March 2027. First, reported EPS roughly doubles, from EUR 1.05 to about EUR 2.13, as the fair-value noise from the ORNANE disappears; stock screens will show "+100%", and the P/E on reported earnings falls from about 39x trailing to about 17x on FY2027, which can widen the base of generalist and quantitative buyers. Second, the ROFA purchase price allocation either validates or dents SPIE's reputation as a disciplined acquirer. The events that could change the narrative are the election (which sets the French risk premium), a visibly faster German organic growth rate, and any step on capital returns.

So what. The 6-to-12-month window brings EBITA upgrades and EPS downgrades at the same events, and the order of events is the practical point. The EPS cuts land between November and March, together with the operating confirmations; the ROFA answer lands in March; the election in April to May; the roadmap in the second half of 2027. SPIE has already de-rated on flat estimates, so the first negative EPS revision breadth in a year could deepen the French discount if investors read it as operating weakness. That window is the one to enter the position through, rather than ahead of.

Where I differ from the market. Consensus expects FY2027 EPS of EUR 3.46 and rising; I expect FY2027 consensus to fall 5% to 7% and EPS estimates to rise again only from FY2028. Bernstein (top pick, target EUR 59.50) and Morgan Stanley (EUR 55, with 4% organic growth) are on the side of operating upgrades, and I agree with them there. Deutsche Bank (EUR 57, with FY2027 EPS of EUR 3.02 on a stricter definition) is the broker whose EPS arithmetic I share.

Counter-case and what would change my view. If most brokers follow the company in adding back the surcharge, and have quietly entered the new share count without publishing (the analyst's second own-research report found four brokers silent for two weeks), the cuts may be smaller and already partly inside the EUR 3.44 mean. What would change my view: FY2027 consensus EPS holding above EUR 3.40 after the March results, with net financial items disclosed near EUR 127m.

Score: 39, set by the Rater. Guidance, which counts most, is likely to be met (about 85%) and firmed at one or two events: a quantified FY2027 margin floor in July, and a 2030 roadmap at the 2027 Capital Markets Day, which may fall at the edge of the window. That is a modest raise against about 8% revenue growth. Consensus EPS, the line that drives the price, should fall 5% to 7% for FY2027 by April as brokers enter the October share count, the two coupons and the surcharge; that is about -0.7 times revenue growth, roughly the 20th percentile of the Universe illustration. Operating upgrades (organic growth, and FY2028 EBITA through EUR 1bn) partly offset the EPS cut. The narrative gets worse before it gets better, with revision breadth turning negative and the Buy share expected to slip. The net effect is a mild negative, below the group's 44 because the dated EPS cut lands inside the window, between Carlsberg's mixed 43 and IMCD's limited 38.

#8 Current momentum: guidance, sell-side, narrative, technicals, and peers

Conclusion: SPIE's operating and guidance momentum is steady to positive and its estimate momentum is flat, while its price, technical and narrative momentum is negative and driven by French country risk; peers with volume inflections have taken the money, leaving SPIE as the unrewarded compounder of its group.

Guidance momentum. Guidance was reiterated, not raised, at both of Holzke's events, and the direction of the margin was confirmed with the comment that SPIE "never wants to give up" margin gains.

Sell-side momentum. FactSet FY2027 EPS revisions are 0% over one month, -1% over three, 0% over six and +4% over twelve; EBITDA revisions are +1%, +2% and +9% over one, three and twelve months; sales are up 4% over twelve months. The mean target price is down 2% over one month and up 4% over six. The share of Buy ratings is 85%: up 18 points over three months (after the Jefferies upgrade in September) and down 7 over one month. The Viewforth dashboard's revision-momentum score is -1, and its pinned letter for sell-side earnings momentum is C. After Q3, Morgan Stanley raised its target to EUR 55 from 54, Bernstein holds EUR 59.50, Jefferies EUR 55 (with FY2027 EPS cut 2%) and Deutsche Bank EUR 57; four brokers have been silent.

Narrative momentum. Bernstein wrote that the Q3 beat "substantially weakens the bear case" on France, and every broker's note explains the share price mainly by the French discount. The dashboard's thematic-fit letter is D and its reading of investor interest is "nonplussed".

Technical momentum. The price of EUR 40.76 sits near the bottom of its 52-week range of EUR 40.10 to 53.06 and 12.1% below its 200-day moving average, with the 50-day average (43.1) below the 150-day (46.1), which is below the 200-day (46.3). Relative strength is at the 17th percentile of the universe, and returns are -13.2% over three months, -14.6% over six and -10.1% over twelve. The pinned letters are C for technical momentum and C for valuation. Co-movement with the ten dashboard peers explains only 22% of SPIE's daily share-price variance (beta 0.71), down from 35% in August: 78% of the move is specific to SPIE, and that specific part is French yields.

Peers. Investors have paid for volume inflections, turnarounds and the makers of scarce equipment, not for steady compounders with a French listing. Bravida and Instalco have re-rated on volume inflections in a Nordic building recovery; Bilfinger warned in September; Fasadgruppen is the roll-up gone wrong; Renew is the other "evidence improved, shares did not" name; Arcadis and MBB trade near SPIE's multiple. The table gives the figures.

Inference and so what. SPIE's momentum is negative where the share price is set (the multiple, the technicals, the French listing) and neutral to positive where earnings are set (operating revisions, guidance). That split matches the Sector Digest's "rising estimates under a flat multiple" setup, with the twist that SPIE's multiple is not flat but falling, for a reason outside the company. The low beta to peers (0.71) cuts both ways: a sector de-rating (a write-down at a principal contractor such as Bravida, or a data-centre financing freeze) would hurt SPIE less, and a sector re-rating would help it less. SPIE's momentum will turn on French news, not sector news.

Where I differ from the market. The crowded Buy consensus (85%) and the falling price are not a contradiction that the market has resolved; together they are an asymmetry. The Buy-rated brokers treat the bear case qualitatively and do not model it, so the first downgrade with a quantified bear case could move the shares more than its news warrants. I therefore read the current momentum readings as a reason for patience on timing, not as a verdict on the case.

Counter-case. Momentum regimes persist. The 200-day average has risen in 9 of the last 12 months, so a price base is forming rather than formed. What would change my view: the 50-day average crossing back above the 200-day with relative strength above the 40th percentile, or the spread of French ten-year government bonds (OATs) over German Bunds falling back under 100 bps.

Score: 52, set by the Rater. One measure is barely positive and one is in the bottom fifth, which gives C. The parts lean negative without contradicting the measures strongly enough to move the letter. Guidance was reiterated, not raised. FY2027 EPS revisions were 0%, -1% and 0% over one, three and six months, against +1% to +9% on EBITDA, and the Buy share is up 18 points over three months. The price is 12% below the 200-day average, with the 50-day below the 150-day below the 200-day; returns are -13% to -15%; and French yields dominate the narrative. The comparable peers split, with Bravida and Instalco strong and Bilfinger weak. So the topic sits at the floor of the band.

#9 Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts and the case

Conclusion: the operating case is simple and well founded, with a narrow range of EBITA outcomes and an EPS range whose direction is predictable; it carries one large exogenous risk that is dated, trackable and hedgeable, and one unverified acquisition price that will be settled on 5 March 2027.

Simplicity of the case. Six drivers decide the case: three above EBITA (German grid conversion; the acquisition engine and its prices; French stabilisation) and three below (financial cost, the tax surcharge, the share count). The level of SPIE's earnings is spread across close to 30,000 customers and 1,000 branches, with 85% of revenue visible at the start of the year, so it is predictable. The change in earnings against history is concentrated in the six drivers, and the three below EBITA are the most certain figures in the forecast: contractual coupons, shares already issued and enacted tax. The case is therefore predictable at the EBITA line, and predictable in direction at the EPS line.

The range of FY2027 outcomes (model basis). FY2027 EBITA ranges from about EUR 905m in the bear case to about EUR 1,000m in the bull case, around a base of EUR 959m: about 10% from end to end, skewed slightly upward. The bear case assumes organic growth of 1.7% and then 1%, 20 bps of margin leaking to subcontractors, ROFA's EBITA halved and no further deals. The bear case needs three things to go wrong at once. The bull case assumes 4% organic growth as public money arrives early, an 8.1% margin and EUR 500m of deals. A sudden-shock bear case, a French sovereign crisis freezing private capex together with a data-centre financing freeze, takes EBITA to about EUR 870m (-9%), using the decremental margin of 2020.

FY2027 adjusted EPS ranges from about EUR 2.80 to EUR 3.40 around EUR 3.15: about 18% from end to end. Over the next twelve months the risk is skewed slightly downward, by the surcharge, by a financial run-rate EUR 5m to 10m higher than modelled, and by ROFA's automotive clients. Beyond 18 months it is skewed upward, by bolt-on acquisitions and the option to return capital.

The five judgements that move the shares most, with the arithmetic if each is wrong by a plausible amount. The multiple (A) is worth four to ten times any of the earnings judgements (B to E) over 18 months. B is the judgement the model is most confident is right. C and D are one judgement in two guises. E is the one that could change the quality rating rather than the earnings.

Risks by suddenness, trackability and materiality. The one large risk, a French sovereign spike, is sudden but dated, trackable and hedgeable; the other risks are moderate, gradual or remote. The matrix sets them out, and two further facts size them. Project-loss precedents in the sector are Caverion (EUR 59m), Eltel (EUR 55m) and SPIE's own UK business (EUR 8m in 2017). Rothschild Redburn expects European automotive capex to fall sharply after 2028, which is the main gradual risk to ROFA's order intake.

Sector and cyclicality precedents. SPIE fits the template of the sector's operational outperformers, and it has already lived through its own version of the sector's main failure. The sector's underperformers fall into three groups: acquisition-led growth masking organic weakness with leverage (SPIE itself in 2015 to 2020 after the SAG acquisition, Fasadgruppen's rights issue, Instalco's margin falling from 8% to 5.9%); project write-downs (Caverion, Eltel); and collapses in framework call-offs in process industry (Bilfinger in 2026, -44%). The outperformers have scarce crews on repricing contracts, customers whose asset bases grow, self-funded consolidation and cash discipline, all of which describe SPIE. SPIE's 2020 test (revenue -4.8%, margin down to 5.1%, cash held) shows that its cyclicality is shallow at the cash line. The sector's share-price rule of the last two years, that volume inflections get paid and compounders do not, is the one rule on which SPIE currently sits on the wrong side.

Disclosure for monitoring. Quarterly organic growth by segment is exactly the right variable for tracking the operating thesis. Margins, the EPS bridge, ROFA and the backlog are disclosed only half-yearly or not at all, so the EPS thesis can be checked only in March and July. The seven milestones below will confirm or break the case.

Where I differ from the market. The sell-side treats the French factor as a discount to be looked through. I treat the French factor as the case's dominant risk, large but dated and hedgeable, and the EPS bridge as the case's small risk, near-certain and dated. The market has the sizes the other way round.

Score: 64, set by the Rater. Fundamentally the case is simple and constrained. The FY2027 EBITA range is about 10% from end to end and the EPS range EUR 2.80 to 3.40 around 3.15 (about -11% and +8%), skewed slightly down. 85% of revenue is visible at the start of the year, 86% of debt is at fixed rates with leverage heading from 1.75x towards 1x, and the 2020 test showed shallow cyclicality at the cash line. The below-EBITA drivers are contractual. Two things widen the share-price outcome: a sudden but dated, trackable and hedgeable French sovereign binary (10% to 15% off the price around the April to May 2027 election), and the ROFA price, unverified until 5 March 2027. The topic sits in line with the groups (60, 62), with a narrower range than Shell (59) and just below OEM International (65), whose range is similarly narrow but which faces no political binary.

#10 Where the stock is in its lifecycle

Conclusion: SPIE is bottoming on the multiple, turning up at EBITA and about to stall for two quarters at EPS; the thesis broadens after March 2027 and the election, not before.

Evidence. The dashboard's rule places SPIE in the "Bottoming" phase. The two-year-forward P/E has fallen from a two-year median of 13.7x (and 15.7x in February 2026) to about 11.7x, the 16th percentile of the last two years, the 28th of five years and about the 49th of ten. The price is near its 52-week low, under a downward-sloping stack of moving averages. Operating momentum has turned, with organic growth of -0.9%, +3.1% and +4.7% in the three quarters of 2026. Estimate momentum is flat and about to dip at EPS, and guidance momentum is "met, not raised". The next new positive is dated (German public money reaching revenue from 2027), as are the next binary event (April to May 2027) and the next narrative reset (the 2027 Capital Markets Day).

Inference: three speeds.

  • On the multiple, the stock is bottoming. The de-rating has covered more than half the distance from the two-year median to the crash band. The remaining fall to a fair trough multiple (9.9x to 10x, or EUR 32 to 35 a share) is about 15% to 20% and would require a lasting French shock.
  • At EBITA, the business is turning up. The organic growth trough is behind it, and the 2026 acquisition cohort consolidates fully in 2027.
  • At EPS consensus, the stock is about to stall for two quarters because of the mechanical cut, without any operating cause.

The thesis broadens only after March 2027, once ROFA is verified, consensus EPS is rebased and reported EPS has normalised. It broadens more clearly after the election, when investors can pay for the German grid story without a French haircut, and it could reinforce in the second half of 2027 with the roadmap and the first discussion of capital returns.

So what. SPIE is a bottoming stock whose turn has a calendar. The catalysts that end the bottoming are exogenous and dated, and the one company-controlled event in the window, the FY2026 results, carries a negative optical element (the EPS cut) alongside positive ones (reported EPS doubling, ROFA clarified). A bottoming reading argues for using the lower bands of the fair-multiple range for the 18-month horizon, as the guideline does, and for buying in tranches around the known dates rather than all at once.

Where I differ from the market. Bernstein and Jefferies treat the stock as already turning up ("stronger foundations for 2027"; "bear case weakened"); Morgan Stanley and Deutsche Bank treat the French factor as the swing factor. I agree that the business is turning up, but the stock is not yet turning, and neither the Q3 sales nor the March results alone will turn it.

Counter-case and what would change my view. A budget passed in December with narrowing spreads could pull the turn forward by a quarter; a hard-left candidate in the May run-off could extend the bottoming into 2028. What would change my view on the phase: two consecutive quarters of relative strength above the 50th percentile with the 50-day average above the 200-day, or FY2027 consensus EPS stabilising above EUR 3.30 after March.

Score: 52, set by the Rater. The computed Bottoming phase is right for the stock but understates the business. The multiple has fallen from 13.7x to 11.7x and the price sits near its 52-week low below a falling stack of averages, while organic growth has already turned (-0.9%, +3.1%, +4.7% through 2026). The next six months bring a stall in EPS consensus with no operating cause, before the thesis broadens after March 2027 and the election. A turn-up with a calendar is better than BP's late Reinforcing phase (50) but below Indutrade's Bottoming (57), where the turn was already hinting in orders and no dated cut stood in the way.

#11 The fair multiple

Conclusion: the guideline fair multiple of about 10.5x to 10.9x is a trough-band discipline appropriate to the Bottoming phase; my view of the fair multiple after the election is the ten-year median of 11.8x, with 9.9x as the floor case and 12.9x as the stretch case.

Evidence: the ten-year range. Excluding outlier months, SPIE's two-year-forward P/E over ten years has a 10th percentile of 9.9x ("crash"), a 30th of 10.94x, a 35th of 11.2x ("conservative"), a median of 11.8x ("prudent"), a 75th of 12.9x ("defendable") and a 90th of 14.0x ("mania"). The five-year median is 12.3x, the two-year median 13.7x, and the multiple now is about 11.7x.

Evidence: the guideline. The model's return of record is computed at the guideline fair multiple of 10.49x, "reached at the 18-month column". The Phases page, as at 3 November, gives the guideline for the Bottoming phase as 10.94x (the 30th percentile), 6% below the multiple now.

Evidence: the history. Over the last decade the multiple ran at 9.5x to 11x in 2018 to 2020 (the years of SAG dilution, leverage above 3x and the 2017 UK write-down), at 11x to 13x in 2021 to 2024 as margins rose from 5.1% to 7.6%, and at 13x to 15.7x from 2025 to mid-2026, before the French de-rating. Brokers' discount rates in their DCF valuations have risen to 8.25% to 9%.

My view. The guideline's discipline is right for a Bottoming stock: forecasts are more uncertain in this phase, the catalyst is exogenous, and the lower bands guard against paying for a turn before it is confirmed. Within the guideline range, I hold that 10.94x (the Phases figure), rather than 10.49x, is the better anchor for the 18-month horizon, for three reasons.

  1. The business is demonstrably better than in the years that set the bottom decile: the margin is 260 bps higher, leverage is a third of 2017's, SPIE is investment grade, and it has a two-to-three-year grid backlog. A multiple below 10x therefore requires a lasting shock rather than the base case.
  2. Net of the French factor, the current multiple already sits at roughly the ten-year median. Morgan Stanley puts SPIE's long-run forward P/E at 12.5x, in line with the average since its IPO.
  3. The 2024 precedent: French-listed contractors recovered their multiples within months of political clarity, with earnings estimates barely changed.

My central estimate of the fair multiple twelve months after an election that does not destabilise France is the ten-year median of 11.8x, with 12.9x reachable if the roadmap and a capital-return step arrive together; my floor case is the crash band at 9.9x. For the 18-month horizon I would use 10.94x as the guideline and show 11.8x as the base case after the election, which is what #12 does.

Where I differ from the market. The sell-side's median target of EUR 57 implies about 15x to 16x the brokers' own FY2027 EPS, a return to the highs of 2025 to 2026. I think that band was a passing premium, paid during the wave of enthusiasm for the power needs of data centres, and not the fair level for a compounder growing 3% organically. At the other extreme, the dashboard's valuation letter C and the guideline's lower band encode a near-trough multiple that prices in French risk. I think the fair level over 18 months sits between those two views, at the prudent band.

Counter-case and what would change my view. If the surcharge becomes permanent, French politics stays unstable through 2028 and the ROFA allocation disappoints, the conservative band (11.2x) rather than the median is fair. If the election delivers a stable majority and spreads under 80 bps, the five-year median of 12.3x becomes the reasonable base within a year.

Score: 57, set by the Rater. Neutral readings on both measures give C. I place it a little above the middle of the band because the peer reading leans slightly cheap and the business is plainly better than in the 2018 to 2020 years that set the bottom of the range (margin +260 bps, leverage a third of 2017's, investment grade). It stays well below the band's top because the Bottoming phase and the coming EPS cut argue for the memo's 10.9x guideline rather than the 11.8x median, and on the model's lower EPS the stock already trades at about 12.0x, a touch above the median.

#12 Total shareholder return

Conclusion: at the guideline trough multiple, the 18-month return is about +3% and the three-year return about +18%, all of it from earnings and dividends net of a give-back on the multiple; at the ten-year median multiple, the same earnings give about +15% and +31%, so the multiple, not the earnings, is where this case's reward and its timing both sit.

The model's return of record. At the guideline multiple of 10.49x and from a starting price of EUR 41.18, the model's return to 31 December 2027 is +2.7% (+2.3% annualised), for a value of EUR 42.31 a share; its return to 30 June 2029 is +17.9% (+6.3% annualised), for a value of EUR 48.54. The model's printed split of that return into dividends, multiple and earnings is distorted by a basis break in its EPS history, explained in the end notes, although the totals are right. On a clean, like-for-like basis, the start is the model's own two-year-forward EPS of EUR 3.44 at about 12.0x, and the end is EUR 3.83 at 10.49x.

Over three years, the same three parts are about +25% from earnings (EPS rising to EUR 4.29), about -13% from the multiple and about +8.5% from dividends, giving about +18%.

About half of the multiple's give-back is simply the model's lower EPS being recognised. The model's quoted starting multiple of 11.3x is on consensus EPS; on the model's 9% lower FY2027 EPS, the stock trades at about 12.0x. The other half of the give-back comes from the guideline multiple sitting 6% to 7% below today's multiple.

What drives the return. Earnings do the work, and the multiple takes most of it back. The earnings leg is the well-founded part: EBITA grows 9% to 10% a year, EPS 8% to 9%, and dividends 8% to 12% at a 40% payout. The multiple leg is the trough-band assumption, which is the right discipline for a Bottoming stock but the wrong forecast if the election passes without a shock. The sensitivity of the return to the multiple is therefore the whole story.

The return is asymmetric. The floor case costs about 3% over 18 months, because the dividend covers most of a further de-rating to the crash band; the prudent case earns about 15%; and the three-year return is positive in every row, because earnings and dividends compound through a flat or falling multiple. On consensus EPS rather than the model's, each row is about 4 points higher at 18 months, and my input changes in #6 add about one point to each row.

Downside about 3% at the crash-band floor; about +15% at the ten-year median; positive in every row over three years.

Where I differ from the market. The sell-side's EUR 57 median target is a 40% return at a multiple I do not think is fair; the model's +2.7% is a return at a multiple I think is a floor. My central 18-month expectation is +12% to +15%, most of it after the election, and my three-year expectation is near +30%.

Counter-case and what would change my view. A hard-left or gridlocked election outcome would hold the multiple in the crash-to-conservative band through 2028, and the 18-month return would be zero to low single digits including the dividend. A 2027 recession, applying the 27% decremental margin, would cut the earnings leg by 5% to 10%. What would change my view: the OAT-Bund spread (above 175 bps for a quarter, or below 80 bps), and FY2027 consensus EPS after March.

Score: 52, set by the Rater. The memo's central expectation gives C, and on the scale +12% to +13% maps to about 55. I move it down to 52 because the path depends on a re-rating that hangs on the French election. Weighting the memo's own multiple table gives only about +10%, and the return of record at the guideline multiple is +3%. The lower tail is thin, though: the 9.9x floor costs only about 3% because dividends cover it, and the three-year return is positive in every row.

#13 Summary conclusion

Build the position around the known dates, not before them: the EPS cut to April 2027, the ROFA answer on 5 March 2027, the election in April to May 2027.

SPIE is the best-run large multi-technical services company in Europe and the purest listed way to own the German grid build-out. Its cash engine, built on negative working capital and cash conversion above 100% for a decade, funds a proven consolidation model without new equity. SPIE's earnings are moving in the right direction and will keep doing so: EBITA grows about 10% in each of the next two years and passes EUR 1bn in 2028, within a narrow range of outcomes that leans slightly upward, because 85% of each year's revenue is visible, costs flex, pricing passes through and the company has a clean record of meeting the floors it sets. The share price has detached from those earnings: SPIE has de-rated by 20% since June on flat estimates, driven by French sovereign yields, although 68% of its revenue comes from outside France.

Two dated issues make the case less crisp. First, adjusted EPS will grow 2 to 3 points more slowly than EBITA through FY2027, because of SPIE's own 2026 financing (3.37m new shares and two bonds at 3.875% and 4.875%) and the extended French surcharge; consensus has not absorbed these costs and will cut FY2027 EPS by 5% to 7% between now and April 2027, while every operating report confirms the case. Second, SPIE bought ROFA at a price that does not reconcile with the stated multiple unless ROFA came with a great deal of cash, and the purchase price allocation on 5 March 2027 will decide whether SPIE is still the disciplined acquirer on which its multiple history was built. Neither issue changes the EBITA path; both shape the next six months.

The practical case is therefore sequenced rather than simple. The guideline trough multiple gives a low-single-digit 18-month return and a high-teens three-year return, all from earnings and dividends. The ten-year median multiple, which I think is fair twelve months after an election that does not destabilise France, gives about +15% and +31%. The reward is in the multiple, and the multiple's catalyst is the French presidential election in April to May 2027. Waiting for the EPS cut to pass and the ROFA answer to arrive costs little, and the French factor can be hedged against Eiffage or VINCI in the meantime. SPIE is a position to build around the known dates, not before them.

End notes

Definitions and basis. "EBITA" is the company's adjusted EBITA. "EPS" is adjusted EPS on the company basis, with the French tax surcharge treated as a cost unless stated. "Net debt" is the company's figure, excluding leases. The price is EUR 40.76 at 23 October 2026; the model's return uses EUR 41.18 at 21 October. Two-year-forward P/E is about 11.7x and market value about EUR 7.1bn. The forecasts are the Financial Analyst's model (update 2), with the analyst's two small input changes set out in #6 and in inputs-changed.md.

The basis break in the model's EPS history. The model's history shows FY2025 EPS of EUR 2.08 on the Viewforth definition, whereas its FY2026 figure is on the company's adjusted basis. The model's printed FY2026 EPS growth of "+38.8%" is therefore a basis break, not growth; like-for-like growth from EUR 2.69 is +7.4%.

The distorted split of the model's return. The model splits its return into dividends (+5.1% to December 2027 and +8.5% to June 2029), the multiple (-28.5% and -31.2%) and earnings (+36.6% and +58.9%). The earnings leg is measured from a starting EPS near EUR 2.8 that blends the FY2025 Viewforth-definition figure (EUR 2.08) with the company-basis forecasts, and the multiple leg is correspondingly measured from an inflated starting multiple near 14.7x. The two legs offset each other by about 25 points, so the totals are right; #12 gives the clean split.

Abbreviations and internal terms. ORNANE: a French convertible bond redeemable in cash and/or new or existing shares. RP5: the fifth regulatory period of German electricity-grid regulation. OAT: French government bond; Bund: German government bond. PMI: purchasing managers' index. EPC: engineering, procurement and construction. DCF: discounted cash flow. TSR: total shareholder return. RN: Rassemblement National. pp: percentage points; bps: basis points. "Universe", "dashboard", "Phases page", "Sector Digest" and "pinned letters" refer to Viewforth's internal screening and research tools; the named comparison companies in each score (for example CVS, Linea Directa, OEM International) are reference cases from Richard's and the Rater's prior work.

Visuals. Visuals in visuals/drawn/ were drawn by the Visual Editor, and visuals in visuals/drawn-copy-editor/ by the Copy Editor, from figures stated in the memo; where a chart required arithmetic (the FY2027 EPS bridge, the ROFA price range, the margin added by drop-through, the EBITA growth rates), the method is given under the chart. The five financial tables and the default charts come from FactSet and the Financial Analyst's model (update 3) as built for this memo; the memo text refers to the model's update 2 plus the analyst's two input changes, so small differences between text and default charts are differences of vintage or basis.

Grades: A 90 to 100, B 75 to 89, C 50 to 74, D 25 to 49, F 1 to 24. Scores are set by the Rater.
